en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Thirty, Chapter on Kiṃchanda.
4. The Chaddanta Jātaka:
"Why do you grieve, O lady of shapely limbs?
Why are you pale, though you possess such excellent complexion?"
“You with the large eyes,
you wither like a garland that has been crushed.
“O Great King, I have a pregnancy craving.”
He has indeed attained it in his dream;
such a thing as the longing I have is not easily found.”
“Whatever human pleasures there are,
here in this delightful world—
all those are abundant for me.”
“I shall grant you your longing.
“O King, let all those hunters who are in your realm assemble together.”
"I shall tell you, O Queen,
what my pregnancy longing (dohaḷa) is like.
"These are the hunters for you, O Queen," [he said].
Skilled with the sword, confident,
familiar with the forest and knowledgeable of the wild beasts,
they would have risked their lives for my sake.
“Listen, sons of hunters, as many as are gathered here:
[regarding] the white elephant with six tusks, The white elephant with six tusks, possessing great strength, endowed with all noble marks, and adorned with every auspicious sign.”
I saw it in a dream;
I have need for its tusks,
and if they are not obtained, there is no life for me.”
“Neither by our fathers nor by our grandfathers has a six-tusked elephant ever been seen or heard of;
yet the princess saw one in a dream before Yama.”
"Tell us what kind of noble elephant he is.
"The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions,
above and below— these are the ten directions."
"In which direction does the elephant king stand,
whom Yama saw in his dream as a six-tusked one?
"In the northern direction, straight from here."
Having passed beyond that mountain Sattagiri,
there is the vast and magnificent mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa,
in full bloom and frequented by kimpurisas.
Having ascended the mountain, the abode of the kinnaras,
look down upon the foot of the mountain;
then you shall see one whose color is like a cloud.
There stands the king of banyan trees with eight thousand branches.
There dwells an elephant with six tusks,
entirely white, invincible by others.
Eight thousand elephants with tusks like plowshafts, swift as the wind in their stride, protect him;
they stand watching for any sign of commotion.
They tremble even when stirred by the wind;
yet, seeing one who has become human there,
they would reduce him to ashes, not even his dust remaining.
“In this royal palace, O Queen, there are many ornaments made of gold,
as well as pearls, gems, and those made of beryl.”
What will you do with this ivory ornament?
Do you wish to kill the six-tusked elephant,
or will you have the hunters kill it?
“I am tormented and suffering, O hunter;
I am withering away as I remember him.
O hunter, please do this for me.”
“I will give you five excellent villages.
“Where does he sit? Where does he go?
What is his path when he has gone to bathe?”
"How indeed does that Naga king bathe?
How may we know the destination of the elephant?
"Right there, not far away, is that lotus pond."
The delightful Sutittha and Mahodika,
in full bloom and frequented by swarms of bees—
there indeed that Naga king bathes.
With his head bathed, wearing a garland of lotuses,
all-white and with limbs as fair as the white lotus,
he goes to his dwelling-place in joyful mood.
Having placed the Great Seer, the most auspicious of all, before him,
the hunter, having received those words right there,
took up his quiver and his bow.
The great being Vessavaṇa ascended the lofty mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa,
a rocky abode of the kinnaras.
He looked toward the foot of a mountain;
there he saw a king of banyan trees with eight thousand branches, its color like that of a cloud.
There he saw an elephant with six tusks,
entirely white and difficult for others to overcome;
eight thousand other elephants were guarding it.
With tusks like ivory, possessing the speed and force of the wind,
he saw there nearby a lotus pond,
delightful, with excellent landing places and abundant water.
Where that Nāga king bathes, the lake is in full bloom and frequented by swarms of bees;
having seen the Nāga’s way and his dwelling place, [he spoke].
While he was on his way to the bathhouse, a man of ignoble form appeared from a hidden place,
dispatched by one who follows the dictates of her own heart.
Having dug a pit and covered it with wooden planks,
the hunter hid himself along with his bow;
he waited for the elephant that had come into view with a broad arrow.
The performer of evil deeds was struck down.
Pierced, the elephant let out a terrible cry like a heron,
and all the elephants let out a formidable roar.
Quarreling over grass and wood,
they fled in all eight directions;
clutching at it, each thinking, "I shall kill him!"
He beheld the saffron robe, the banner of the seers;
touched by suffering, this perception arose:
"The banner of the Arhat is beyond reproach by the virtuous."
“He who, being impure, shall wear the saffron robe,
devoid of self-control and truth— ”

He does not deserve the saffron robe who has not vomited out impurity and is not well-composed in the precepts. But he who has vomited out impurity and is well-composed in the precepts— [he is worthy].
Endowed with self-control and truth,
he indeed deserves the saffron robe.
Like an elephant struck by many arrows, [he remains steadfast].
With a mind free from malice, he addressed the hunter:
"For what purpose, for what reason, O friend, have you killed me? To whom does this deed belong?"
“Venerable sirs, she was the chief queen of King Kāsī;
that Subhaddā was honored in the royal court.
She saw him and spoke of me.”
"And he said to me, 'There is wealth in my teeth.
"For many were the magnificent sets of teeth that belonged to my fathers and grandfathers."
That angry princess knows;
the foolish woman, seeking to kill, has committed an act of enmity.
Arise, O hunter, and take up your spear!
“Dante, cut these off before I die!
You should say to that angry princess:
‘A nāga has been slain; here, take its tusks.’”
Rising up, that hunter took a saw and cut off the tusks of that supreme elephant—
tusks that were beautiful, pure, and peerless on earth.
Taking them, he departed from there very swiftly.
Those elephants, terrified by the slaughter and tormented by fear, fled in the eight directions.
Having seen the man, who was a friend to elephants,
they went back to where that Naga king was.
Having cried out and wept there, those Nagas—
Having scattered dust upon their own heads,
they all returned to their respective homes,
placing the Great Sage, the one who is entirely auspicious, at their head.
Having taken the tusks of the supreme elephant—
lovely, pure, and peerless on earth,
with their golden streaks shining all around—
Thus the hunter arrived at Kāsīpura;
he presented the tusks to the princess, saying,
"Behold, these are the tusks of the slain elephant."
Having seen the tusks of that best of elephants from his previous birth as Bhattuppiya,
he crushed her heart right there.
By that very [act], the foolish woman passed away.
Having attained full enlightenment, that one of great power caused coolness to arise in the midst of the assembly.
The bhikkhus, whose minds were well-liberated, asked:
"Buddhas do not manifest themselves without a cause.
What young girl did you see?"
She who then wandered in homelessness, clothed in saffron robes,
was at that time a princess; I,
at that time, was a king of the nagas.
Having taken the tusks of that supreme elephant—
lovely, pure, and peerless on earth—
the hunter went to the city of Kāsī.
Thus indeed was Devadatta at that time.
This ancient conduct, varied and manifold, practiced for a long time through many nights, has not yet vanished.
Free from distress, free from sorrow, and without taints, the Buddha,
having realized it for himself through direct knowledge,
spoke: "At that time, I was..."
"I was there at that time, O monks;
I was then the Nāga king—
thus you should remember this Jātaka."
The Chaddanta Jātaka is the fourth.
